1.transcript: Transcript: The nineteen-oh-seven earthquake, then, and what re-reading the old sheets does to it. Start with the logbook from the Luhemaa station. It is a weather book as much as an instrument book, and that is why it earned its keep. A low background rumble sits on the Luhemaa traces that autumn, and the daily wind and sea entries let us set storm surf aside as its source — the rumble is loudest on flat, still days. The observer's felt account went to a newspaper the same week; the logbook closes in the same year the official history gives; and the crate surfaced through a museum's accession list, not through anything in the logbook. Tammik has argued for two ruptures minutes apart, and Oks thinks the magnitude drops once you model those old instruments. Neither holds: the trace shows one rupture, and the magnitude barely moves. The source sits under the coastal parish the catalogues name. What changes is the damage — the river towns stand on soft alluvium, and that, more than the size of the shock, drew the map of ruin. The sheets survive nearly complete. Hardly a sheet is missing from the years the network changed hands, the years before nineteen fifteen are as thickly covered as any, and each sheet carries its station's stamp. The trouble is framing: someone trimmed the margins off for display, and the time marks went with them. Kolmsaare? I am persuaded. The aftershocks sit along its mapped trend. The northern structure fits the uplift no better, these are not scattered shocks in healed crust, and the Kolmsaare structure is young.
1.stem: [Academic Talk — Seismology] According to the professor, what did the survey of the surviving seismograms show about the collection?

options.A: Roughly half the sheets survive, with the losses concentrated in the years the network changed hands
options.B: The record is thin before 1915, since stations then reused sheets that showed no visible events
options.C: Sheets from three stations were interfiled decades ago, and reattributing them has taken most of the project's first year
options.D: The sheets survive nearly complete, but many were trimmed for framing and lost their margins with the time marks

2.transcript:
Transcript: The Aravik lot - two hundred pieces, bought in nineteen twelve, and a century of muddle since. That muddle has a cause: Pellamaa's day-book. His running numbers show the lot was renumbered at the sale itself, and that explains the two conflicting catalogue sequences. The book is not barren otherwise. It records a partner, but he is named on the first page, and his papers came to us in nineteen forty. Its months run at an even pace, with no slow seasons to read; and the permit-suspension years are, oddly, the book's busiest.

Fibre work next. The lot's ancient repairs use strips cut from a discarded letter, and that letter is now the oldest text we hold. The sheets are of one manufacture throughout. The literary pieces are on fresh sheets, not reused accounts. Ilmsalu checked the register against the trays last spring, expecting parchments booked as papyrus - the register and the trays agree.

So where did the lot come from? Pellamaa built it from several finds, matching pieces by look to make a salable whole. There is no shared damp stain on these sheets. Nor did it come out of a rubbish mound; there is no town soil. Ilmsalu reads the frame marks as an older collection redispersed, a fair reading - but those marks are our own mounting shop's.

Next, the editors go to Norvalt, which bought from the same source in the same season, and try for joins. The documentary texts wait; the cartonnage stays where it is; the concordance of hands is a student's job for later.
2.stem: [Academic Talk — Papyrology] What did the professor say the fiber analysis established about the pieces in the lot?

options.A: A dozen pieces entered in the register as papyrus are parchment, a slip nobody has caught since
options.B: The sheets fall into two manufacturing qualities, mixed indifferently across the documentary and literary pieces
options.C: Repairs made in antiquity used strips from a discarded letter, itself now the oldest text in the lot
options.D: Several literary pieces were written on reused account rolls, with the accounts still legible on the back

3.transcript: Transcript: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Look at the ensemble figures: thirty-two dancers crammed into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of. The ensemble numbers here are not thinned, they are packed. Nor is this a drill book — the roll follows one evening's order straight through — and the entrances are in the same ink and the same hand as the figures, so nobody redrew them for a later season. What does it actually record? The corps, in detail. Their steps are written out in full, each number carried through to its end. The soloists get a line of description apiece, no more. And the mime scenes are passed over in a phrase, where later notations linger on them. Now the wrapper. There is a customs stamp on it, and three articles have built an itinerary out of that stamp. The stamp dates a crate of linen thread, not the roll's journey; the wrapper is freight paper somebody reused, and the address on it has sent people to the wrong city. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. The order of the numbers is not in doubt, so the orchestral parts can wait, the rubbed passages were already read under raking light last winter, and the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project.
3.stem: [Academic Talk — Dance History] What did the professor say the study of the roll's notation established about how much of the dance it records?

options.A: It lays out the floor patterns fully, while the steps themselves are left to a few conventional signs
options.B: It records the corps in detail and reduces the soloists' variations to a line of description each
options.C: It gives the mime scenes at the same length as the dancing, where later notations drop them
options.D: It carries two numbers complete and no more than the opening figures for the rest

4.transcript: Transcript: Sarvela's beetles — eleven thousand pins, and questions the specimens cannot settle. Start with the coastal meadows. The literature says Kepsara's ground beetle vanished around nineteen ten. Rehepapp takes that at face value. Ilves says the older records are misidentified relatives, since the sister species was not split off until the fifties and much of the coastal literature predates the split — a fair worry. But I have been through the trays: the old specimens are there, and they are correctly named. Nor did the beetle shift inland: the drained margins have been swept, and swept well, since the sixties. The post-war sweeping in the meadows themselves amounts to two afternoons. What thins out around nineteen ten is the collecting, not the beetle. The nineteen-oh-four auction catalogue. One copy carries a pencil note naming the buyer, whose heirs gave us the material — that is how the chain closes. Its lot descriptions run to a line each, too thin to match a box against, the prices in it are steep for the day, and the cabinet it lists came to the museum with the rest. The labels. There is no pencil under the ink; one hand wrote the coastal labels and its abbreviations don't vary; the oldest hand is Sarvela's own, from his school years. What the writing shows is a nineteen-thirties re-curation: a good many labels rewritten, the old spellings quietly modernized. Next: not re-pinning, the pins stay where Sarvela put them; not sequencing, we won't cut them; not the traded duplicates, Vaher published that list years ago. The mites that ride on these beetles — nobody has looked.
4.stem: [Academic Talk — Entomology] What is the professor's assessment of the claim that the beetle disappeared from the coastal meadows early in the twentieth century?

options.A: He suspects the species moved into the drained margins nearby, where nobody thought to sweep
options.B: He argues the apparent disappearance tracks where collectors went, not where the beetle lived
options.C: He thinks the older records rest on misidentified relatives, so there is no disappearance to explain
options.D: He is persuaded, noting that later collectors worked the same meadows hard and came back without it

5.transcript: Transcript: Vaissalu's drawings, set beside the stones that still stand. He drew some forty memorials in the seventeen nineties; nine of those stones survive. The comparison isn't flattering. The letterforms he gives are wrong in the same places an earlier antiquarian, Rennik, had gone wrong — same bind-runes, same swallowed vowel. He was copying Rennik's sketchbook, not the stone. Two things he's innocent of, mind: where a stone had flaked, he leaves a gap, honestly blank; and his churchyard attributions hold up wherever we can test them. How did I come to this? The parsonage at Kolgama. I catalogued its library as a student, one wet summer, and there was Rennik's sketchbook. That's the whole connection — no squeezes have ever come out of that house, the glebe wall there is nineteenth-century brick, and Kolgama's own pastors kept none of the visitation books that first mention the stones. The dating quarrel now. Hallik dates the group later than the years carved on it. I'd narrow that. One carver, the Ansu master, worked late, and his pieces colour how the rest get read; I would not extend that to the group. The formulas are common regional ones, older than any printed model I know, and the stone there weathers fast, so I don't rest a case on weathering. Twenty-odd stones are unlocated. We won't print a text nobody has seen on the stone, and they stay in the corpus volume, marked missing. A handlist goes to the county museums; some may sit unrecognized in a storeroom. The radio appeal was tried upriver and turned up little but field boulders.
5.stem: [Academic Talk — Epigraphy] Why does the professor bring up the parsonage at Kolgama?

options.A: Its glebe wall was rebuilt with fragments from two of the stones, which is how those pieces survived
options.B: Its successive pastors kept the visitation books in which the stones are first mentioned
options.C: Its attic held the bundle of paper squeezes, found again when the roof was renewed in the 1960s
options.D: The professor once catalogued its library, an aside about how he came to the material in the first place

6.transcript:
Transcript: Kaldevere's garden, laid out in the seventeen nineties, and the question that comes first: was it Nurmsaar's? The design is his; the hand shows in the sweep of the approach. But I doubt he came. The plans travelled by post, and were adapted on site by whoever held the spade. The estate books enter no payment for a visit; his pupil's planting lists, which Harm compares with the beds, are a poor match; and the family were naming Nurmsaar in their own letters within two years of the digging, not a generation after.

Now the drawings against the ground. Harm reads the showpiece drawing as a tidied presentation piece, symmetrical on paper and loose in the soil, and I would believe that elsewhere. Here the bed edges we dug out in ninety-four sit where the drawing puts them, foot for foot, through the first campaign. Then it was set aside within a decade, as taste turned. The same sheet governs the park and the walled ground alike, and there is no rival drawing to braid it with.

The nursery invoices. Substitutions run right through them: Parnaste sent hardier kinds than the ones ordered. They date the water garden where the guidebooks do; they are made out to the steward; and the estate's own nursery supplied little beyond seed.

Tiidema's letter-book, last. It is a thin thing - a handful of letters, there are no blotting pages bound in, and his famous quarrel is not in it. What it does is show him at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was fetched from abroad.

options.A: It shows he trained at Kaldevere from boyhood, against the story that he was hired from abroad
options.B: Its blotting pages preserve impressions of letters sent, including several the family later destroyed
options.C: His weekly letters to the absent family amount to a garden diary nobody meant to keep
options.D: It records his running quarrel with a neighboring estate's gardener, the professor's favorite thread in the archive

7.transcript: Transcript: Turvaste — three parish volumes, and the crisis years at their centre. What the registers show is not a parish dying evenly. The burials fall heavily on households that had arrived within the previous decade, cottagers, hired men, families off the road, while the long-settled farms came through comparatively lightly. Not departure: the town lists show no bulge of arrivals from here in those years. Not two waves either — the burials run in one long swell. And the hamlets and the church village lost at much the same rate. Now, the entries. Halliste built a good deal on the cause column, and Piir on the lists at the back, both worth having: each says the register shapes what we think we see. But the cause column runs right through the crisis, and stillbirths are entered in the main sequence. The entries give a name and a farm, and leave the messenger out. The close reading shows the clerk wrote up several days at a time, so the day-by-day dating everyone quotes is ours, not the parish's. The eighteen-eighties rebinding. The margins came through it uncut, no bill for the work has been found, and the covers went back on plain. What did happen is that a few leaves from the parish upriver were bound in by mistake, and nobody caught it until the nineteen thirties. Next? Not the rent rolls, Turvaste's burned in the eighteen forties. Not the neighbours, whose registers are in poor shape. Grain prices are already in the appendix of my first article. I want the slow method: reconstituting a sample of households in full.
7.stem: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] What does the professor imply the project will take up next?

options.A: Extending the same reading to the neighboring parishes whose registers survive in fair shape
options.B: Linking the register families to the manor's rent rolls to follow survivors across the crisis
options.C: Bringing in the grain price series to test how the crisis lines up with the harvests
options.D: Reconstituting a sample of households in full, a slower method she has argued the material can support

9.transcript:
Transcript: Kuivalinn hall came down in nineteen sixty-one. What survives is Rebasmaa's notebooks, eleven recordings, and Nommiste's drawings. Rebasmaa measured with pistol shots fired from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings. He had asked the mill to send workers in to fill the seats; the mill declined, so the hall stood empty for both sittings. What he entered are the single readings themselves, not averages; no cards stand behind them. The hall was renovated in fifty-four and he did not go back, so that book holds one campaign, not two.

Was the sound as fine as its reputation? I think so: a modern designer would still envy the measured values. The memoirists came late and added little. The resident orchestra was a middling band that toured to no acclaim. And these figures are not the long reverberation that period taste supposedly prized - they are short and defined.

Now the recordings. Cleaned digitally, they can anchor a computed model of the room, which no drawing on its own could support. The players were shifted between takes with no note kept, so the discs will not fix anybody's placement, and the room's contribution sits well above the surface noise once cleaned. The studio discs are a different decade and a different orchestra.

Next, then. Rebuilding a length of that wall at full scale was costed and is beyond us; the museum will mount its exhibition without our help; the local press we have read through already. Nommiste's smaller hall at Harmavere still stands, and we will measure it as our stand-in.

options.A: She thinks the reputation grew after the demolition, fed by memoir writers mourning the building
options.B: She credits it, and points to measured values that a modern designer would still envy
options.C: She reads the fame as a period taste for long reverberation that later audiences stopped prizing
options.D: She ties the fame to the orchestra in residence, whose sound traveled with it on tour

11.transcript:
Transcript: Soorna is a small brown lake with a deep archive: Virkland's notebooks from the eighteen nineties, the fishermen's association minute-books, and our series since eighty-eight.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

Kivrand argues the darkening began centuries before the first surveys. I reject that. Those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is - and Soorna's level has shifted. So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

Back on the water: the outflow gauge is Tammiste's project; the neighbouring lakes were sampled in ninety-six and written up; the landowners have asked to be kept off the boats. Our first job is Virkland's sunken marker buoys, whose positions carry his depth grid.
11.stem: [Academic Talk — Limnology] Why does the professor mention the minute-books of the fishermen's association?

options.A: Their complaints about net fouling give dated sightings of the weed beds the surveys missed
options.B: They show the catch was weighed at the landing for decades, a series long enough to be worth mining
options.C: An argument written up in them preserves where the association believed the springs entered the lake
options.D: They record the association paying Virkland's boatman, which fixes the survey seasons the notebooks leave vague

Transcript: Kuivalinn hall came down in nineteen sixty-one. What survives is Rebasmaa's notebooks, eleven recordings, and Nommiste's drawings. Rebasmaa measured with pistol shots fired from the stage, logged position by position across two evenings. He had asked the mill to send workers in to fill the seats; the mill declined, so the hall stood empty for both sittings. What he entered are the single readings themselves, not averages; no cards stand behind them. The hall was renovated in fifty-four and he did not go back, so that book holds one campaign, not two.

Was the sound as fine as its reputation? I think so: a modern designer would still envy the measured values. The memoirists came late and added little. The resident orchestra was a middling band that toured to no acclaim. And these figures are not the long reverberation that period taste supposedly prized - they are short and defined.

Now the recordings. Cleaned digitally, they can anchor a computed model of the room, which no drawing on its own could support. The players were shifted between takes with no note kept, so the discs will not fix anybody's placement, and the room's contribution sits well above the surface noise once cleaned. The studio discs are a different decade and a different orchestra.

Next, then. Rebuilding a length of that wall at full scale was costed and is beyond us; the museum will mount its exhibition without our help; the local press we have read through already. Nommiste's smaller hall at Harmavere still stands, and we will measure it as our stand-in.

21.transcript: Transcript: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. 30.transcript: Transcript: Sarvela's beetles — eleven thousand pins, and questions the specimens cannot settle. Start with the coastal meadows. The literature says Kepsara's ground beetle vanished around nineteen ten. Rehepapp takes that at face value. The post-war sweeping in the meadows themselves amounts to two afternoons. What thins out around nineteen ten is the collecting, not the beetle. The nineteen-oh-four auction catalogue. One copy carries a pencil note naming the buyer, whose heirs gave us the material — that is how the chain closes. Its lot descriptions run to a line each, too thin to match a box against, the prices in it are steep for the day, and the cabinet it lists came to the museum with the rest. The labels. There is no pencil under the ink; one hand wrote the coastal labels and its abbreviations don't vary; the oldest hand is Sarvela's own, from his school years. What the writing shows is a nineteen-thirties re-curation: a good many labels rewritten, the old spellings quietly modernized. Next: not re-pinning, the pins stay where Sarvela put them; not sequencing, we won't cut them; not the traded duplicates, Vaher published that list years ago. The mites that ride on these beetles — nobody has looked.

Transcript: Soorna is a small brown lake with a deep archive: Virkland's notebooks from the eighteen nineties, the fishermen's association minute-books, and our series since eighty-eight.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

Kivrand argues the darkening began centuries before the first surveys. I reject that. Those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is - and Soorna's level has shifted. So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

Back on the water: the outflow gauge is Tammiste's project; the neighbouring lakes were sampled in ninety-six and written up; the landowners have asked to be kept off the boats. Our first job is Virkland's sunken marker buoys, whose positions carry his depth grid.

33.transcript: Transcript: The Vantsi roll — nine metres of notation, and the question everyone asks first: which staging is this? My answer is the plain one. It is the first staging. Look at the ensemble figures: thirty-two dancers crammed into the downstage third, exactly the crowding the opening reviews complained of. The ensemble numbers here are not thinned, they are packed. Nor is this a drill book — the roll follows one evening's order straight through — and the entrances are in the same ink and the same hand as the figures, so nobody redrew them for a later season. What does it actually record? The corps, in detail. Their steps are written out in full, each number carried through to its end. The soloists get a line of description apiece, no more. And the mime scenes are passed over in a phrase, where later notations linger on them. Now the wrapper. There is a customs stamp on it, and three articles have built an itinerary out of that stamp. The stamp dates a crate of linen thread, not the roll's journey; the wrapper is freight paper somebody reused, and the address on it has sent people to the wrong city. Wrapper and roll are of a piece, the same decade, and the stamp is a western port's. Next? We are going to dance it. One suite, with students, in the spring — the performance is the test. The order of the numbers is not in doubt, so the orchestral parts can wait, the rubbed passages were already read under raking light last winter, and the ballroom manuals are somebody else's project.
33.stem: [Academic Talk — Dance History] What is the professor's position on the claim that the roll records the ballet as it was first staged?

options.A: She reads it as a teaching document, setting down what dancers were drilled on rather than any staging given
options.B: She endorses the claim, finding in the ensemble figures the crowded groupings the first reviews complained of
options.C: She endorses it for the figures, though she takes the entrances to have been redrawn for a later season
options.D: She reads the roll as a record of the revival, with the ensemble numbers already thinned

34.transcript: Transcript: Turvaste — three parish volumes, and the crisis years at their centre. What the registers show is not a parish dying evenly. The burials fall heavily on households that had arrived within the previous decade, cottagers, hired men, families off the road, while the long-settled farms came through comparatively lightly. Not departure: the town lists show no bulge of arrivals from here in those years. Not two waves either — the burials run in one long swell. And the hamlets and the church village lost at much the same rate. Now, the entries. Halliste built a good deal on the cause column, and Piir on the lists at the back, both worth having: each says the register shapes what we think we see. But the cause column runs right through the crisis, and stillbirths are entered in the main sequence. The entries give a name and a farm, and leave the messenger out. The close reading shows the clerk wrote up several days at a time, so the day-by-day dating everyone quotes is ours, not the parish's. The eighteen-eighties rebinding. The margins came through it uncut, no bill for the work has been found, and the covers went back on plain. What did happen is that a few leaves from the parish upriver were bound in by mistake, and nobody caught it until the nineteen thirties. Next? Not the rent rolls, Turvaste's burned in the eighteen forties. Not the neighbours, whose registers are in poor shape. Grain prices are already in the appendix of my first article. I want the slow method: reconstituting a sample of households in full.
34.stem: [Academic Talk — Historical Demography] What is the professor's central claim about what the Turvaste registers show for the crisis years?

options.A: Deaths were concentrated among recent arrivals, while long-settled families came through comparatively lightly
options.B: The parish lost people mainly to departure, with households leaving for the towns rather than dying
options.C: Losses fell hardest on the outlying hamlets, while the church village itself was less touched
options.D: The crisis came in two waves a year apart, and the second was the heavier one

35.transcript: Transcript: The nineteen-oh-seven earthquake, then, and what re-reading the old sheets does to it. Start with the logbook from the Luhemaa station. It is a weather book as much as an instrument book, and that is why it earned its keep. A low background rumble sits on the Luhemaa traces that autumn, and the daily wind and sea entries let us set storm surf aside as its source — the rumble is loudest on flat, still days. The observer's felt account went to a newspaper the same week; the logbook closes in the same year the official history gives; and the crate surfaced through a museum's accession list, not through anything in the logbook. Tammik has argued for two ruptures minutes apart, and Oks thinks the magnitude drops once you model those old instruments. Neither holds: the trace shows one rupture, and the magnitude barely moves. The source sits under the coastal parish the catalogues name. What changes is the damage — the river towns stand on soft alluvium, and that, more than the size of the shock, drew the map of ruin. The sheets survive nearly complete. Hardly a sheet is missing from the years the network changed hands, the years before nineteen fifteen are as thickly covered as any, and each sheet carries its station's stamp. The trouble is framing: someone trimmed the margins off for display, and the time marks went with them. Kolmsaare? I am persuaded. The aftershocks sit along its mapped trend. The northern structure fits the uplift no better, these are not scattered shocks in healed crust, and the Kolmsaare structure is young.
35.stem: [Academic Talk — Seismology] What is the professor's central claim about what the re-analysis changed in the picture of the 1907 earthquake?

options.A: The source lay well out under the sea, not beneath the coastal parish the catalogues name
options.B: What was catalogued as one shock was two ruptures minutes apart, blended together in contemporary accounts
options.C: The magnitude comes down appreciably once the old instruments' exaggerated response is taken into account
options.D: The damage pattern owed more to ground conditions in the river towns than to the size of the event

36.transcript:
Transcript: Soorna is a small brown lake with a deep archive: Virkland's notebooks from the eighteen nineties, the fishermen's association minute-books, and our series since eighty-eight.

The minute-books first: they settle a dating problem. The association paid Virkland's boatman by the day, and the payments are dated, fixing the seasons his notebooks leave vague. Their other contents are thin. The net-fouling complaints are undated grumbles; the argument about the springs names no location, being a quarrel over payment; and the catch was weighed at the landing for two years before the practice lapsed.

Virkland's transparency readings against ours. They scatter too widely to carry a trend - to his credit the notebooks say why, listing wind and cloud for each cast. The scatter is not a steady offset. His figures run deeper on some days and shallower on others, in the bays and on the open water alike, and matching him week for week does not tighten the cloud.

Kivrand argues the darkening began centuries before the first surveys. I reject that. Those proxies move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever colour the water is - and Soorna's level has shifted. So I am not dating the onset a little later than Kivrand does, I am not pushing it further back on the pollen and charcoal, and I am not calling the darkening periodic either.

Back on the water: the outflow gauge is Tammiste's project; the neighbouring lakes were sampled in ninety-six and written up; the landowners have asked to be kept off the boats. Our first job is Virkland's sunken marker buoys, whose positions carry his depth grid.
36.stem: [Academic Talk — Limnology] How does the professor respond to Kivrand's argument that the darkening of Soorna's water began centuries before the first surveys?

options.A: He rejects it, arguing the signals Kivrand relies on move whenever a lake's level shifts, whatever the water's color
options.B: He endorses it, and takes the pollen and charcoal work to push the beginning further back still
options.C: He accepts an early start but dates it later than Kivrand does, closer to the received view
options.D: He reads the darkening as periodic rather than a single onset, returning with the wetter centuries
